title: The development of doctrine
hook: Newman: living ideas grow like a tree, staying themselves

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Henry Newman, later a priest of the Oratory, on a ship with no wind. Your line was lead, kindly light. Today, the question Newman was wrestling with when he turned.

An old photograph: a child on a doorstep, gap-toothed, in a too-big sweater. Then the same person decades later. The height, the face, the voice, all different. And yet nobody at the family table doubts it's the same person. Something stayed while everything grew. Newman put a question like that to the whole Church. The first Christians didn't use every word the Church uses now. So is today's Church a different thing wearing an old name? Or the same thing, grown up?
screen: `A CHILD, THEN A GROWN ADULT.` → `THE SAME PERSON?` → `THE SAME CHURCH?`

segments.voice: Newman wrote a long book about it, An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine, in the months before he became Catholic. First, the problem. Some teachings were said in words the first Christians never used. The creed says the Son is of one substance with the Father, a phrase that isn't in the Gospels. Did the Church add something new, or put into words what was there all along? Second, the image. A living idea, Newman argued, grows the way living things grow: a seed becomes a tree. Jesus himself compares the kingdom of heaven to a mustard seed that grows into a tree where birds come to rest. The tree looks nothing like the seed, yet it is the same plant, and no other plant could come from that seed. Third, the sentence. Newman wrote: "In a higher world it is otherwise, but here below to live is to change, and to be perfect is to have changed often." It does not say anything goes. Fourth, the test. Ideas can also decay, the way a body can sicken instead of grow. So Newman tried to describe how to tell a true development from a corruption: a true one keeps the same type and principles, and carries forward what came before instead of overturning it. Catholic teaching today speaks of doctrine developing in this sense. Other Christians describe faithfulness over time in their own ways. For Newman, the question was not whether the Church had changed. It was whether it had stayed itself while growing.
screen: `WORDS THE FIRST CHRISTIANS NEVER USED.` · `A SEED BECOMES A TREE.` · `HERE BELOW TO LIVE IS TO CHANGE.` · `GROWTH, OR DECAY?` · then, large: `TO BE PERFECT IS TO HAVE CHANGED OFTEN.`

segments.voice: Think back to how you understood God, or goodness, or what matters, as a child, a picture, a prayer, a rule, and set it next to how you understand it today. What has changed, and what, under all that change, has stayed the same? If you pray, give thanks for the growth; if you don't, notice the thread that runs from then to now.
Mustard seed. The image Jesus used for a growing kingdom, which Newman borrowed to explain how a true teaching can grow into something unrecognizable and still be the same plant.
Your line: to live is to change. The seed and the tree are one plant. Eight hundred ninety days now.

howItsDone: Catholic theologians and teachers draw on Newman's idea of development when they explain how the Church's teaching is put into new words over the centuries while remaining faithful to what was handed down.

notes: Claims rule: the number of Newman's 'notes' of a true development is left out; the script names only same type, same principles and continuity. Confirm wording.
'Finished it in the months before he became Catholic': confirm (Newman left the Essay unfinished as he was received).
The oak/seed image is the script's illustration of Newman's growth analogy; Newman's own images in the Essay include a stream and the growth of the body. Confirm acceptable.
Exact wording of the Newman quotation: confirm against the 1845 or 1878 edition.
The sentence on other Christians is kept deliberately neutral; check it is fair.
